Front. Environ. Sci., 06 November 2026

Sec. Atmosphere and Climate

Volume 14 - 2026 | https://doi.org/10.3389/fenvs.2026.1993707

Decomposition of carbon emission drivers and urban typology in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area: implications for regional environmental management

  • YW

    Youwei Wan 1

  • XZ

    Xinrui Zhang 1

  • QZ

    Qiping Zou 2*

  • GD

    Guoyong Deng 3

  • 1. School of Economic Management and Law, Jiangxi Science and Technology Normal University, Nanchang, China

  • 2. Explosives Corporation Limited, Changsha, Hunan, China

  • 3. Maiju Technology Group Co., Ltd., Xiong’an, Hebei, China

Article metrics

View details

Abstract

The Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area is marked by pronounced urban heterogeneity, so that a uniform account of its carbon emission drivers is unlikely to hold. Using panel data for 11 cities from 2015 to 2023, this study applies the Generalized Divisia Index Method to decompose eight drivers of emission change and to classify the cities by their factor contribution structures. Economic growth (G) and output carbon intensity (CI) are the largest positive and negative contributors in ten of the eleven cities (mean G = +19.18%, mean CI = −9.94%), the exception being Macao. An exploratory Ward clustering of the four most variable factors, cross-validated against k-means, distinguishes four types of driving structure—carbon-intensity suppression, economic-scale driven, energy-scale expansion, and a specialized service-structure type (Macao); an innovation index combining research and development (R&D) intensity and patent density varies independently of these types. Decoupling is likewise uneven, ranging from strong decoupling in three cities (Foshan, Zhongshan and Hong Kong; Tapio elasticity t = −0.152 to −0.437) to weak decoupling in six (0.133 ≤ t ≤ 0.462) and expansive coupling in Huizhou and Macao. Per-capita emissions and energy-structure carbon intensity show marked dispersion. These findings inform a three-tiered policy discussion—differentiated measures, collaborative governance, and data support—for coordinated low-carbon governance in urban agglomerations.

1 Introduction

Global climate change poses a severe challenge to sustainable development, and the Paris Agreement has forged a broad consensus on a green, low-carbon transition. In 2020, China announced its “dual carbon” goals—peaking carbon emissions by 2030 and achieving carbon neutrality by 2060—which hinge on progressively decoupling economic growth from carbon emissions. Because urban agglomerations concentrate both economic activity and energy use, understanding their differentiated carbon-emission drivers is central to operationalising the dual-carbon strategy.

The Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA) is one of China’s major development platforms and comprises the “9 + 2” configuration of nine mainland cities and two Special Administrative Regions. Its member cities differ markedly in industrial structure, development stage, resource endowment, and institutional system. These differences imply that the driving structure of carbon emissions is unlikely to be uniform across the region and that a single, undifferentiated mitigation policy is unlikely to be effective. A systematic, city-level comparison of emission drivers is therefore needed.

From a methodological standpoint, Index Decomposition Analysis (IDA) is a classic tool for quantifying emission drivers, and the Logarithmic Mean Divisia Index (LMDI) is its mainstream variant (Ang, 2005); however, the product-form construction of LMDI fixes the factor set in advance: at most one absolute quantity can enter as the leading term of a single product chain, and the remaining factors must enter as ratios. The Generalized Divisia Index Method (GDIM) addresses both points through a system of constraint equations that captures the intrinsic relationships among factors (Vaninsky, 2014); a detailed comparison of the two methods is given in Section 2.1.

The validity of GDIM has been demonstrated across sectors and scales—from China’s mining sector (Shao et al., 2016) and the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei region (Yan and Yin, 2017) to the Yangtze River Delta (Wan et al., 2025a), the Southwest region (Wan et al., 2025b), and international comparisons between China and the United States (Zhang N. et al., 2022). The framework has also evolved beyond historical attribution: combined with Monte Carlo simulation and LSTM networks, it has been used to project industrial carbon-peaking windows (Li et al., 2023) and to assess carbon lock-in risks in urban buildings (Shi et al., 2026); it has also been extended to VOC emissions (Zhu et al., 2025) and, when coupled with decoupling indicators, to energy-related PM2.5 emissions (Yu and Fang, 2021), industrial carbon decoupling (Shen et al., 2024), and regional grouping strategies (Chen L. et al., 2025). These studies confirm GDIM’s suitability for multi-factor, interrelated systems, but they do not provide a unified decomposition framework covering all GBA cities.

Existing GBA-related research has approached the issue from several directions. One stream identifies emission drivers using regression-based tools such as machine learning (Qiao et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025) and geographically weighted regression (Chen M. F. et al., 2025); while informative, these approaches do not quantify each driver’s contribution to changes in emissions. A second stream examines energy transition and reduction efficiency (Zhang P. F. et al., 2022) and draws international decoupling comparisons (Xie et al., 2025; Qiao and Wu, 2025). A third stream develops urban typologies using aggregate or efficiency indicators (Ramaswami et al., 2018; Tong et al., 2018; Zhong et al., 2021; Kuncheria et al., 2025; Xing et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Chen J. et al., 2025); these classifications describe the “external manifestations” of low-carbon development rather than the “internal driving logic” of emission change. Finally, several GBA-specific studies have examined transport (Wang et al., 2023), building operations (Tang et al., 2025), CO2–VOC synergy (He et al., 2025), county-level urban expansion (Ming et al., 2024), collaborative governance (Wu, 2025), spatiotemporal evolution (Wang S. J. et al., 2026) and city–industry relations (Li X. J. et al., 2022), yet none applies a unified decomposition framework to the whole GBA city cluster.

Three research gaps therefore remain. (1) Methodological gap. GDIM, which is capable of handling multi-factor constraints, has not been systematically applied to all cities of the GBA, leaving the region without a unified, comparable decomposition. (2) Classification gap. Existing city classifications rely mainly on aggregate or efficiency indicators (e.g., GDP, industrial structure) and do not incorporate the contribution structure of emission drivers, so they cannot reveal the underlying logic of emission change across cities. (3) Policy-alignment gap. Research on collaborative governance is largely qualitative and lacks an empirical basis for aligning quantitative decomposition results with differentiated mitigation strategies.

To address these gaps, this study applies GDIM to the complete “9 + 2” city cluster using panel data from 2015 to 2023, decomposing the eight drivers of carbon-emission change over 2016–2023. Its objectives are: (1) to quantify the contribution of the eight factors (G, CI, E, CSI, P, PC, PG, EI) to emission change in the GBA and its constituent cities; (2) to classify the 11 cities according to the contribution structure of these drivers; and (3) to outline a three-tiered policy discussion—differentiated measures, collaborative governance, and data support—for the GBA’s low-carbon transition.

This study contributes in three respects. Methodologically, it extends the application of GDIM to a highly heterogeneous megaregion. Empirically, it derives an empirical typology of low-carbon development in the Greater Bay Area from the contribution structure of driving factors rather than from aggregate indicators: the types are obtained by formal clustering, their labels follow the driving dimensions that define them, and innovation intensity is examined as a separate dimension rather than being built into the type names. Practically, it links the decomposition results to the binding target of reducing CO2 emissions per unit of GDP, offering a reference for regional collaborative governance.

2 Research methods and data

2.1 Method selection and theoretical basis

Several families of methods can be used to analyse the drivers of carbon emissions, and they differ in the type of question they can answer. Structural Decomposition Analysis (SDA) is informative but requires input–output tables, which are not available annually for all GBA cities. STIRPAT-type and panel-regression models are well suited to estimating the elasticity of emissions with respect to socio-economic covariates, but they return marginal effects rather than an exact, additive attribution of the observed change in emissions and depend on functional-form assumptions. Index Decomposition Analysis (IDA) addresses precisely the latter question, and the Logarithmic Mean Divisia Index (LMDI) has become the mainstream IDA variant because it is residual-free and easy to interpret (Ang, 2005).

However, LMDI is built on the product form of the Kaya identity, and this fixes the factor set in advance: the terms must form a single product chain that exhausts the identity, so only one absolute magnitude can enter as the chain’s leading term, while the others are absorbed into ratios and cannot stand as separate factors on an equal footing with them. Because that identity is exactly identified, LMDI also has no mechanism for enforcing several accounting constraints at once, which is what the eight-factor system used here requires. These are limitations of capability rather than of accuracy: a driver left outside the chosen identity is not merely estimated less precisely under LMDI, it is absent from the decomposition altogether.

The Generalized Divisia Index Method (GDIM) overcomes both limitations. By introducing a system of constraint equations that encodes the intrinsic relationships among factors, GDIM allows absolute and relative indicators to be analysed within one framework and separates the contributions of mutually related factors without double counting (Vaninsky, 2014). This makes GDIM the most suitable method for the present study: its analytical object is the contribution structure of all eight drivers (G, E, P, CI, CSI, PC, PG, EI), including the absolute-magnitude drivers (G, E, P), of which a single LMDI product chain can carry only one as its leading term, the rest being absorbed into ratios, and the urban typology in Section 3.3 depends on exactly this structure. The choice is therefore dictated by the requirements of the analysis rather than by convenience.

2.2 Model construction of GDIM

The Generalized Divisia Index Method (GDIM) provides a rigorous mathematical framework for analyzing multi-factor driven systems (Vaninsky, 2014). Its core lies in attributing changes in the target variable (carbon emissions) to the combined effects of multiple interrelated explanatory variables. Compared to traditional index decomposition methods (e.g., LMDI), GDIM achieves an unbiased decomposition of contributions in complex systems by introducing intrinsic constraint equations among factors.

2.2.1 Fundamental principles of GDIM

Assuming that the target variable (e.g., carbon emissions) can be expressed as a function of influencing factors (Equation 1):

2.2.2 Introduction of constraint equations

However, in real-world socioeconomic systems such as the Greater Bay Area, economic growth, energy consumption, and population mobility are not independent but deeply interconnected. Decomposition that ignores these interrelationships may lead to bias. To characterise the combined effects of multiple absolute and relative factors concerning economic growth, energy transition and population agglomeration across the Greater Bay Area, this study extends the conventional decomposition framework by expressing carbon emissions along three interrelated pathways—economic output, energy consumption, and population size—as follows (Equation 6):

This multi-path expression defines carbon emissions from three distinct dimensions and lays the foundation for incorporating multiple absolute factors. To address the interdependence among these factors, the GDIM framework introduces constraint equations that capture the intrinsic relationships among them (Vaninsky, 2014):

The five identities in Equation 7 characterise the interdependent relationships among economic output, energy consumption and population size: the first equates the economic and energy pathways of CO2, the second the economic and population pathways, the third the energy and population pathways, the fourth defines per capita output (PG = G/P), and the fifth defines energy intensity (EI = E/G).

Its matrix form is given by Equation 8:

Under these constraints, the contribution decomposition formula for the total change is revised as:

In Equation 9, is the Jacobian matrix of of order ( constraint equations and variables in this study, hence 5 × 8); is the Moore–Penrose generalized inverse of ; and I is the 8 × 8 identity matrix. This formula guarantees that for systems with mutually constrained influencing factors, the decomposition results can not only precisely quantify the independent contribution of each driving factor, but also fully comply with the inherent constraint logic of the system.

The intuitive implication of Equation 9 is that, under constrained conditions, the variation of factor is not fully flexible. Instead, its effective variation direction is projected onto the tangent space of the constraint surface. With the projection matrix, the redundant contributions derived from the intrinsic correlation among variables are eliminated. Accordingly, the net contribution of each influencing factor to the variation of the target variable can be accurately obtained.

Applicability Note to the Greater Bay Area: The general decomposition framework provided by Equation 9 lays a solid methodological foundation for quantifying the differentiated carbon emission driving patterns among cities in the Greater Bay Area, which arise from discrepancies in industrial structure, energy structure, and development stage. In the subsequent sections, based on this framework and combined with the economic-energy-population data of the “9 + 2” cities in the Greater Bay Area, a specific carbon emission decomposition model will be constructed.

2.2.3 Computational implementation and closure check

The decomposition was implemented in R (version 4.3.2). The Jacobian was evaluated analytically from the constraint system at each observation; the Moore–Penrose generalized inverse was computed with MASS::ginv(), and the projection matrix was formed explicitly. The path integral was evaluated by summing over consecutive years, using the trapezoidal rule on the projected gradient (i.e., the mean of the end-point gradients multiplied by the annual change of each factor), which reproduces the discrete sum requested for panel data. Because the constraint projection removes the redundant contributions arising from the intrinsic correlation among the variables—that is, from the accounting identities that link them—the eight factor contributions are additively exact: across all 88 city–year units (11 cities × the eight annual intervals from 2016 to 2023), the largest absolute closure residual is 2 t of CO2 (mean 0.55 t), consistent with the one-tonne granularity implied by the four-decimal storage of the output values (in units of 104 t) rather than with any model misspecification; the full unit-by-unit check is reported in Supplementary Appendix D (Supplementary Table D1).

2.3 Analytical framework: contribution rates, classification and decoupling

Based on the GDIM framework established in Section 2.2, this study applies the eight-factor decomposition to the Greater Bay Area. The classic Kaya identity breaks down carbon emissions into the product of population, per capita GRP, energy intensity and carbon intensity, but it takes population as a single absolute variable and does not independently identify the contributions of the core absolute indicators, including gross regional product (GRP) and total energy consumption (Vaninsky, 2014). The eight driving factor variables defined in this study are presented in Table 1.

As shown in Table 1, the decomposition framework incorporates three key absolute factors: G (economic scale), E (energy scale), and P (population scale), which capture the scale expansion effect of the Greater Bay Area as a core growth pole. Meanwhile, core intensity indicators including CI, CSI and EI are further integrated, allowing quantitative evaluation on the policy effects of carbon intensity and energy intensity constraints under the dual-carbon target. In addition, variables PC and PG help identify the impacts of economic welfare distribution and residential consumption patterns on carbon emissions.

These factors are not mutually independent but are linked by the accounting identities given in Equation 7. Substituting the objective function and the constraint system into the general GDIM formula of Equation 9 yields the contribution of each factor. This system of equations systematically characterises the complex interdependent relationships among economic output, energy consumption, population size, and various intensity indicators.

For the eight variables , the accounting identities in Equation 7 define a system of five constraint equations: , where . The Jacobian therefore has order 5 × 8. Substituting and into the general GDIM formula of Equation 9 yields the projected contribution of each factor (Equation 10).

By substituting the objective function and the system of constraint equations in Equation 7 into the general GDIM Equation 9, the precise contribution values of the above eight factors to the carbon emission change in the Greater Bay Area and its individual cities during 2016–2023 can be calculated. A positive value indicates that the factor serves as a driver of carbon emission growth, while a negative value signifies that it exerts an emission reduction effect.

Contextual Interpretation of the Greater Bay Area: This model is particularly well-suited for analyzing the heterogeneity within the Greater Bay Area. For instance, in service industry-developed cities such as Hong Kong and Shenzhen, the mitigating effect of CI (carbon intensity of output) may be more pronounced; while in manufacturing hubs like Foshan and Dongguan, the reduction in EI (energy intensity) may make a prominent contribution. Through quantitative comparisons within a unified framework, the model enables an understanding of the diverse low-carbon development pathways within the Bay Area.

2.3.1 Definition and calculation of cumulative contribution rate

Based on the aforementioned GDIM decomposition model, the annual contribution of each driving factor to carbon emission changes between adjacent years can be quantified, with the unit of 10,000 t CO2. To identify the cumulative effect of each factor throughout the research period of 2016–2023 and realize horizontal comparability across cities, this study further converts the annual contribution values into the cumulative contribution rate.

Let denote the eight driving factors, where . For city , the cumulative contribution rate of factor over 2016–2023 is defined as Equation 11:

Here, represents the contribution of factor to the change in carbon emissions for city in year (10,000 tCO2); represents the CO2 emissions of city in the base year 2015 (10,000 t).

sums factor 's annual contributions over 2016–2023 and divides by the city’s 2015 emissions. Fixing the denominator at the 2015 baseline gives every city and every factor the same benchmark, so the rates can be compared across cities and across factors. Because the denominator is the base-year level rather than the total emission change, the eight rates of a city sum to that city’s overall rate of change in CO2 over 2016–2023 rather than to 100%.

CI, CSI and EI are composite ratios defined by accounting identities, and their variation therefore jointly reflects industrial composition, energy mix, efficiency and the statistical boundary of the data. The decomposition reports the contribution of each ratio to the change in CO2, that is, an association within the identity rather than the isolated effect of a single mechanism. A decline in CI is reported as an intensity-related mitigation effect and is not evidence of technological progress as such.

2.3.2 Formal classification of driving structures

The eight factor contributions are linked by the identities used to construct them and are not statistically independent: four eigenvalues of their correlation matrix are effectively zero, and E and CI are almost collinear across cities (r = 0.95). Entering all eight into a distance-based classification with eleven observations would therefore be unstable.

The clustering input was restricted to the four factors with the largest between-city dispersion—E, CI, EI and PC, with standard deviations of 12.85, 9.69, 9.64 and 7.78 percentage points—each standardised to zero mean and unit variance. Cities were grouped by Ward’s hierarchical method with squared Euclidean distances (Ward, 1963). K-means with 200 random restarts run on the same matrix returns identical partitions at every k (adjusted Rand index = 1.00; Hubert and Arabie, 1985).

The number of groups was selected from the merge schedule, with the internal-validity indices reported alongside it in Supplementary Appendix E—the Calinski–Harabasz index (Caliński and Harabasz, 1974), the silhouette coefficient (Rousseeuw, 1987) and the Davies–Bouldin index (Davies and Bouldin, 1979). With eleven observations these indices exclude solutions with five or more groups but do not discriminate reliably among smaller numbers of groups, so the choice of four rests on the merge schedule, whose decisive discontinuity is reported in Section 3.3. Type labels were assigned ex post from the group centroids on the eight original factors.

The partition was then examined in two ways: jackknife re-runs omitting one city at a time (Hennig, 2007), and re-estimation under three dimension-reduction schemes (all eight factors; the four-factor scheme; the first two principal components). Given the sample size, the typology is read as an exploratory ordering of cities along two driving axes rather than as a hard partition; the groups that are stable across all checks are identified in Section 3.3.

2.3.3 Decoupling elasticity (Tapio index)

To assess whether economic growth has been decoupled from carbon emissions within a formally recognised framework, this study adopts the decoupling elasticity index proposed by Tapio (2005), , where and denote the relative changes in CO2 emissions and gross regional product between two periods. Eight states are distinguished following Tapio (2005): strong decoupling , weak decoupling , expansive coupling , expansive negative decoupling , and, symmetrically, strong negative decoupling, weak negative decoupling, recessive coupling and recessive decoupling when output stagnates or declines . The Tapio index is a dimensionless elasticity and is conceptually distinct from the cumulative contribution rate defined in Section 2.3.1, which is normalised by base-year emissions; the two measures are therefore reported separately and are not compared on a common percentage scale.

2.4 Data sources and processing

To guarantee the reliability, consistency and comparability of empirical data, this study compiles balanced panel data for the “9 + 2” cities in the Greater Bay Area covering the period 2015–2023. All raw data are retrieved from authoritative official statistical sources. Data sorting and carbon emission accounting are implemented following the principles of transparency and reproducibility. Rigorous pretreatment is conducted to address missing values, differences in statistical scope and other data anomalies.

2.4.1 Data sources

This study involves three categories of core data: socioeconomic data, energy consumption data, and accounting coefficients.

2.4.1.1 Socioeconomic data

The Gross Regional Product (GRP) and year-end permanent resident population data of the nine mainland cities are sourced from the Guangdong Statistical Yearbook and the statistical yearbooks of each city. Hong Kong’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and population data are obtained from the Census and Statistics Department of the Hong Kong Government. Macao’s GDP and population data are derived from the Macao Statistics and Census Bureau.

2.4.1.2 Energy consumption data

The total energy consumption and fuel-specific consumption (including coal, petroleum products, natural gas, etc.) of the nine mainland cities are retrieved from the statistical yearbooks of each city. For Hong Kong, the terminal energy consumption by fuel type (coal, petroleum products, natural gas, electricity) is sourced from the Hong Kong Energy Statistics Yearbook. For Macao, the terminal energy consumption by fuel type (automotive gasoline, diesel, heavy fuel oil, gaseous fuels, etc.) is obtained from the Macao Statistics and Census Bureau.

2.4.1.3 Accounting coefficients

Energy-to-standard-coal conversion factors are taken from Appendix 4 of the China Energy Statistical Yearbook (2023). Carbon emission factors for fossil fuels are derived from the National Greenhouse Gas Emission Factor Database (2nd Edition) and the IPCC (2006) default methodology, and are expressed in tCO2 per tonne of standard coal equivalent (tCO2/tce); these factors are treated as time-invariant (Table 2). Emission factors for electricity are time-varying: year-specific grid emission factors for Guangdong, Hong Kong and Macao are adopted for 2015–2023 (Table 3), thereby reflecting the continuous decarbonisation of the regional power grids.

2.4.1.4 Official emission inventory (cross-validation data)

Hong Kong publishes an official greenhouse-gas inventory, released annually by its Environment and Ecology Bureau. Because this official series is reported in CO2-equivalent and on a territorial (local-source) basis, it differs in gas coverage and accounting boundary from the pure-CO2, energy-consumption-based accounting adopted in this study. It is therefore used solely as an independent reference to cross-validate the magnitude and trend of Hong Kong’s self-accounted emissions (Section 3.5.5), rather than being substituted into the decomposition model.

2.4.2 Carbon emission accounting method

In accordance with the sectoral reference approach specified in the 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories, this study adopts a unified formula to calculate terminal CO2 emissions for each city:

Here, Ei denotes the consumption of energy source in tons of coal equivalent (tce), and refers to the CO2 emission factor of the -th energy type (tCO2/tce).

The emission factors entering Equation 12 are specified in the preceding subsection: fossil-fuel factors are time-invariant and electricity factors are year-specific, with detailed parameters presented in Tables 2, 3.

Because energy statistics are compiled on different statistical bases across the eleven jurisdictions, two nested accounting boundaries are explicitly distinguished and applied consistently in the decomposition.

Boundary B1—Total energy consumption (denominator). For six mainland cities (Guangzhou, Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Huizhou, Jiangmen and Zhongshan), Hong Kong and Macao, the total final energy consumption is the jurisdiction-wide figure published in the official yearbooks: for the mainland cities, the “total energy consumption” reported in the energy chapter (primary energy consumption, i.e., inclusive of energy transformation and transmission losses); for Hong Kong, the territory-wide end-use energy consumption by fuel in the Hong Kong Energy Statistics Yearbook; for Macao, the territory-wide final energy consumption by fuel published by the Statistics and Census Service. For the remaining three mainland cities—Foshan, Dongguan and Zhaoqing—the yearbooks continuously publish only the comprehensive energy consumption of industrial enterprises above designated size; this industrial total is therefore used as a proxy for total energy consumption. This proxy systematically understates the absolute level of energy consumption—and hence of CO2 emissions—in these three cities, because energy use in the residential, commercial and transport sectors is not covered, and it may weaken the characterisation of non-industrial drivers (see Section 4.3).

Boundary B2—Fuel-mix structure (numerator shares). City-level yearbooks do not release society-wide consumption for each individual fuel. For all nine mainland cities, the fuel-mix shares are therefore estimated from the category-specific consumption of industrial enterprises above designated size and applied to the corresponding total energy consumption under a structure-similarity assumption; Hong Kong and Macao use their officially published fuel-specific data directly. Implementation proceeds in three steps: (1) obtain the physical volume of each fuel consumed by industrial enterprises above designated size from each municipal yearbook and compute its share in the industrial total; (2) assuming that the society-wide fuel-mix structure is consistent with that of the industrial sector, apply these shares to the city-level total energy consumption; (3) convert the resulting physical volumes into 10,000 tce using the conversion factors of the China Energy Statistical Yearbook and calculate CO2 using the coefficients in Tables 2, 3.

Treatment of the boundary difference. Only Boundary B1 differs across the sample, and only for Foshan, Dongguan and Zhaoqing. Because the GDIM decomposition is estimated independently for each city (each city’s result depends solely on its own 2015–2023 series), this boundary difference does not affect the per-city decomposition of the other eight cities; it only shifts the cross-city descriptive statistics and the typology, which are sample-dependent. Accordingly, the eleven-city sample is retained as the main specification, and a robustness check excluding Foshan, Dongguan and Zhaoqing is reported in Section 3.5, together with an explicit statement of the limitations in Section 5.3.

2.4.3 Key data processing and harmonization

Unification of Currency Units and Price Base. To ensure cross-city comparability, all economic data are expressed in Renminbi (RMB) at current prices. GRP for the nine Guangdong cities is originally compiled in RMB and used as reported; for Hong Kong and Macao, whose GDP is reported in Hong Kong Dollars (HKD) and Macao Patacas (MOP) at current prices, the values are converted into RMB using annual average exchange rates (Hong Kong dollar: National Bureau of Statistics of China, 2024; Macao pataca: Monetary Authority of Macao, 2024), with the sources and the year-by-year rates for 2015–2023 listed in Supplementary Appendix C (Supplementary Table C1).

Handling of Missing Data: Data on the total social energy consumption of Guangzhou in 2023 is missing. Based on a strong linear trend model established using its data from 2015 to 2022 (,, where is the year index), the 2023 value is estimated to be 6559.61 ten thousand tons of standard coal. The detailed estimation process is provided in Supplementary Appendix B.

Research Scope, Time Period and Modeling Software: 1. Research Scope: This study covers all 11 cities in the Greater Bay Area. 2. Time Period: The model is operated based on panel data from 2015 to 2023, focusing on decomposing the driving factors of carbon emission changes from 2016 to 2023. Key indicator data for the base year (2015) and the end year (2023) are provided in Supplementary Appendix A. Modeling Software: The solution of the GDIM model and the calculation of contribution rates are programmed and implemented in the R language (Version 4.3.2) environment.

3 Results

3.1 Overall characteristics of carbon emission drivers in the Greater Bay Area

This section analyzes the driving patterns of carbon emission changes at the overall level based on cumulative contribution rate data of 11 cities in the Greater Bay Area from 2016 to 2023. Table 4 summarizes the descriptive statistics of the contribution rates of the eight major driving factors, revealing the dominant forces and basic characteristics of carbon emission evolution in the region.

To more intuitively present the distribution differences and outlier characteristics of each driving factor, this study further plots boxplots for the contribution rates of the eight major driving factors.

According to Table 4 and Figure 1, the driving structure of carbon emissions in the Greater Bay Area exhibits the following three prominent characteristics:

FIGURE 1

First, economic growth and carbon-intensity reduction form a pair of opposing dominant factors. The economic scale effect (G, mean 19.18%) acts as the major driver of carbon emissions and is the largest positive contributor in ten of the eleven cities, the only exception being Macao, where the energy-scale effect (42.06%) is larger; economic growth therefore remains the fundamental driving force for the increase in carbon emissions in the Greater Bay Area. In contrast, the output carbon intensity effect (CI, mean −9.94%) exerts an inhibitory effect in most cities, while Macao (+16.93%) is the only region with a positive value, implying that its carbon intensity is still rising. This push–pull pattern constitutes the basic contradiction that determines the overall trend of carbon emissions in the Greater Bay Area.

Second, the effects of energy-related factors and demographic and social factors show significant divergence. The standard deviations of energy consumption scale (E) and energy structure carbon intensity (CSI) are 12.85 and 6.46, respectively, with opposite signs between their minimum and maximum values, reflecting substantial heterogeneity in energy-driven patterns across the Greater Bay Area. For instance, Macao demonstrates a strong promoting effect from energy consumption scale (42.06%) due to its unique industrial structure, whereas Hong Kong shows an inhibitory effect (−4.07%). Shenzhen is the only city with a positive energy structure carbon intensity (+4.57%), in sharp contrast to Macao’s large negative contribution (−21.38%). Similarly, per capita carbon emissions (PC) have a high standard deviation of 7.78, with contributions ranging from −6.84% in Zhongshan to 19.95% in Huizhou, spanning both negative inhibition and strong promotion. This reveals considerable disparities in the per capita carbon performance among cities.

Third, the inhibitory effects of per capita output and energy intensity are relatively limited. The absolute values of the average contribution rates of per capita output (PG, mean −1.94%) and energy intensity (EI, mean −3.55%) are much lower than that of the dominant inhibitory factor CI, indicating that the emission reduction contributions from rising per capita wealth and improved macro energy efficiency remain relatively weak at the current stage. Macao shows exceptionally strong inhibitory effects in both factors (PG = −15.80%, EI = −32.56%), which is associated with its extremely high per capita GDP from the gaming and tourism industry and its relatively intensive energy use pattern, representing a special case.

These findings are consistent with existing studies. A GDIM decomposition of global commercial buildings revealed that economic scale is the primary positive driver, while carbon intensity is the main inhibitory factor (Chen L. et al., 2023), which is highly consistent with the “dual dominant factors” finding of this study. A study on 232 Chinese cities also confirmed that GDP and energy intensity are key driving factors (Zhang et al., 2025). Additionally, a study on the synergistic effect of pollution reduction and carbon emission reduction in 295 Chinese cities found that approximately 51.5% of the cities achieved synergy (Liu et al., 2024). This regional heterogeneity characteristic echoes the differentiated pattern of driving factor contributions among cities in the Greater Bay Area observed in this study.

3.2 Full picture of the driving structure: a visualization analysis based on heatmaps

To visually present the full picture of contribution rates of the eight driving factors across the 11 cities in the Greater Bay Area, this study constructs a heatmap.

As shown in Figure 2, the driving structures of individual cities display significant divergence. From a horizontal perspective, economic growth (G) and output carbon intensity (CI) are the dominant positive and negative drivers across all cities, forming the fundamental contradiction that determines carbon emission evolution. From a vertical perspective, Macao presents a deep red color in energy consumption scale (E, 42.06%), deep blue in energy structure carbon intensity (CSI, −21.38%), and also deep blue in per capita output (PG, −15.80%) and energy intensity (EI, −32.56%), forming a unique pattern of “high energy consumption coupled with strong inhibition”. Shenzhen is the only city showing a red color in CSI (+4.57%), reflecting its relatively slow progress in clean electricity transition. Huizhou displays deep red colors in both economic growth (G, 28.23%) and per capita carbon emissions (PC, 19.95%), revealing the dual pressures of growth-led expansion and rising per capita carbon emissions. These extreme values anticipate the grouping that emerges from the formal classification in Section 3.3.

FIGURE 2

3.3 Classification of urban types based on driving structure characteristics

Section 3.2 shows that the contribution structures of individual cities differ widely. To establish whether these differences form distinguishable groups, the eleven cities were classified with the procedure described in Section 2.3.2, that is, Ward. D2 agglomerative clustering on the four factor contributions with the largest between-city dispersion (E, CI, EI and PC), standardised to unit variance and measured by squared Euclidean distance. The merge schedule is the decisive evidence for a four-group solution. The largest merge distance within the four-group solution — 0.362, in units of the increase in the within-cluster sum of squares on the standardised variables—is about thirteen times smaller than the distance at which the four groups first fuse with one another (4.651). Fewer groups are either uninformative or conflate distinct structures: at two groups the sample separates into Macao and the remaining ten cities, and at three groups the five economic-scale driven cities merge with the four carbon-intensity suppression cities, whose per capita carbon effects have opposite signs (+3.88% and −5.59%; Table 5). More than four groups are ruled out by the internal-validity indices, which deteriorate markedly for , and by the isolation of single cities. The same partition is reproduced by k-means (adjusted Rand index = 1.00). The full merge schedule and the validity indices are reported in Supplementary Appendix E (Supplementary Tables E1, E2).

Three groups of cities remain together under every setting examined: Shenzhen and Zhuhai; Foshan, Zhongshan and Hong Kong; and Dongguan, Jiangmen and Zhaoqing. Guangzhou changes group under each of the three dimension-reduction settings and is treated as a boundary case; Huizhou separates as its own group only under the four-factor scheme; and Macao separates from all other cities under every setting. The typology is therefore read as an ordering of cities along two driving axes—economic scale and per capita carbon pressure—rather than as a hard partition, and the four types below are named after the driving dimensions that define them.

Figure 3A shows the eleven cities in the space of the clustering input, and Figure 3B orders them along the two dominant driving axes, economic scale (G) and per capita carbon effect (PC).

FIGURE 3

Based on this classification, the study selects a representative city from each type (Foshan, Shenzhen, Huizhou and Macao) and plots clustered bar charts of the eight factor contribution rates for each, so as to compare the complete driving structures of the four types.

3.3.1 Carbon-intensity suppression type: mitigation led from the intensity margin

This group comprises Guangzhou, Foshan, Zhongshan and Hong Kong. Its centroid combines the strongest output-carbon-intensity effect of the four groups (CI = −15.90% on average) with the lowest per capita carbon effect (PC = −5.59%) and below-average economic and energy scale (G = 14.57%, E = 1.48%).

The members span a wide range of economic structures, from Guangzhou’s diversified service economy to Foshan’s manufacturing base, and from Zhongshan’s light industry to Hong Kong’s mature service economy. What they share is a strong intensity effect, not a common innovation profile: the group extends across all three innovation strata defined in Section 3.3.5.

Two features of the group deserve emphasis. First, its intensity effect is not uniform in magnitude: Foshan records the largest absolute output-carbon-intensity effect in the whole sample (CI = −18.05%), followed by Hong Kong (−15.91%) and Guangzhou (−15.67%), while Zhongshan’s is −13.97%. Second, the group contains the region’s most mature service economy: Hong Kong combines the region’s lowest economic-scale effect (G = 10.87%) with a strong intensity effect and an energy-scale effect that has turned negative (E = −4.07%), so that its total energy consumption has begun to decline. A service economy’s carbon trajectory evidently depends on which margin the service economy in question operates on—a point returned to in Section 3.3.4.

3.3.2 Economic-scale driven type: growth outpacing intensity gains

This group comprises Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Dongguan, Jiangmen and Zhaoqing. Its centroid records the highest economic-scale effect among the multi-city groups (G = 21.39%) together with a comparatively weak carbon-intensity effect (CI = −11.89%) and a positive average per capita carbon effect (PC = +3.88%): expansion, in short, still runs ahead of the intensity response.

The group merges cities that a reading based on economic scale alone would place in two different categories, namely, Shenzhen, Zhuhai and Dongguan on the one hand and Jiangmen and Zhaoqing on the other. On the driving dimensions that define the clusters these five cities are more alike than a scale-only reading suggests; on innovation intensity, by contrast, they are the most heterogeneous group in the sample (Section 3.3.5).

The group also contains the clearest single-city anomaly of the study. Shenzhen records the only positive energy-structure carbon-intensity effect in the Greater Bay Area (CSI = +4.57%): against a highly electrified economy and clustered high-end manufacturing, the low-carbon upgrading of its power supply system has lagged, so that indirect emissions from electricity continue to rise. For a city with this profile the binding constraint lies on the energy-supply margin rather than on the intensity margin.

3.3.3 Energy-scale expansion type: the huizhou case

Huizhou forms a single-city group. Among the nine mainland cities it combines the largest energy-scale effect (E = 26.15%) with the highest per capita carbon effect in the region (PC = 19.95%) and the weakest carbon-intensity restraint (CI = −3.25%): expansion on every volume margin, with little restraint from the intensity side. Its economic-scale effect (G = 28.23%) is also the highest in the region. The structure points to a prominent risk that per capita carbon emissions will continue to rise alongside economic expansion, and to a severe carbon lock-in risk if green access thresholds are not imposed on new industrial capacity.

Huizhou separates as its own group under the main four-factor scheme but not under the principal-component scheme, where it joins Shenzhen and Zhuhai (Supplementary Appendix E). Its position should therefore be read as the extreme end of the scale axis rather than as a category of one.

3.3.4 Specialized service-structure type: Macao

Macao separates from all other cities at every clustering setting examined and forms a single-city group. Its profile has no analogue among the manufacturing-oriented cities: the energy-scale effect (E = 42.06%) and the output-carbon-intensity effect (CI = +16.93%) are both positive, while per capita output (−15.80%), energy intensity (−32.56%) and energy-structure carbon intensity (−21.38%) are all strongly negative. Macao is thus the only city in the region with a positive CI value and the largest positive carbon-intensity effect in the whole region; specified on a year-by-year basis rather than as a single constant coefficient, this positive effect becomes even more pronounced, indicating that Macao’s economic expansion has been accompanied by a marked decline in carbon productivity.

Macao thus presents a distinctive transition path. The gaming and tourism industries drive a dramatic expansion of energy consumption scale, which acts as the dominant promoting factor. At the same time, benefiting from the rapid substitution of power-generation fuel from heavy oil to natural gas, Macao achieves a strong inhibitory effect on energy-structure carbon intensity; it also shows strong mitigation performance in terms of per capita output and energy intensity. The result is a developmental pattern of high energy consumption under multi-dimensional strong carbon constraints.

Hong Kong does not share this group. Its driving structure—the region’s lowest economic-scale effect (G = 10.87%) against a strong intensity effect (CI = −15.91%) and a negative energy-scale effect (−4.07%) — places it with Guangzhou, Foshan and Zhongshan in Section 3.3.1. The contrast between the two Special Administrative Regions is itself informative: both are service-dominated economies, yet they sit at opposite ends of the carbon-intensity axis, because the clean-energy transition on the supply side, not the service share of output, is what determines their trajectory.

3.3.5 Innovation stratification

To establish whether innovation intensity can serve as a type label, an innovation index was assembled for all eleven cities from two indicators for 2023 — R&D expenditure as a share of GRP and invention patents granted per 10,000 residents—standardised and summed with equal weights (Table 6). The index does not align with the driving-structure types. The economic-scale driven type contains both the most innovation-intensive city in the sample (Shenzhen, index +4.10) and the two lowest within the type (Jiangmen, −1.20; Zhaoqing, −1.49), a within-type range of 5.59 that is the largest of any type, while the carbon-intensity suppression type extends across all three innovation strata.

The cross-tabulation is therefore offered as descriptive evidence alongside the within-type ranges.

3.4 In-depth analysis of core driving factors

3.4.1 Polarization of the per capita carbon emission effect

Per capita carbon emissions (PC = CO2/population) combine total territorial CO2 emissions with the resident population. It measures the aggregate carbon pressure per resident and reflects the combined intensity of production and consumption; because the numerator also covers emissions from industry, power generation, and services, PC cannot by itself isolate household consumption patterns or individual lifestyles. In this study PC is therefore interpreted strictly as a composite per capita indicator, and cross-city differences are discussed alongside each city’s industrial and energy structure.

Huizhou (19.95%) shows the strongest driving effect on per capita carbon emissions, followed by Macao (5.34%), Zhaoqing (5.14%), Jiangmen (5.08%), Shenzhen (4.69%), Zhuhai (2.36%) and Dongguan (2.14%). It indicates that per capita carbon pressure has risen markedly alongside economic expansion and urbanization in these regions. In contrast, Zhongshan (−6.84%), Foshan (−6.65%), Hong Kong (−6.58%) and Guangzhou (−2.28%) present prominent inhibitory effects, revealing that these cities have achieved substantial easing per capita carbon pressure as their economies matured.

This pattern is broadly consistent with the typology of Section 3.3. The economic-scale driven type (Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Dongguan, Jiangmen, Zhaoqing) records positive per capita carbon effects on average, whereas the carbon-intensity suppression type (Guangzhou, Foshan, Zhongshan, Hong Kong) records negative ones; Huizhou, the energy-scale expansion type, is the extreme case (PC = 19.95%).

3.4.2 Diversified paths and contradictions of energy system transition

The contributions of energy consumption scale (E) and energy structure carbon intensity (CSI) reflect distinctly different transition logics and challenges amid heterogeneous resource endowments and industrial structures.

As illustrated in Figure 4, the energy-system transition across the Greater Bay Area spans a wide spectrum rather than following a single path. Macao anchors one end, combining the region’s strongest energy-structure mitigation (CSI = −21.38%) with its only positive output-carbon-intensity effect (CI = +16.93%): the supply side has been transformed, yet carbon productivity has declined. Shenzhen anchors the other end, recording the region’s only positive energy-structure carbon-intensity effect (CSI = +4.57%; Section 3.3.2): carbon productivity continues to improve, but the low-carbon upgrading of the power supply has lagged. The two cases mirror each other and carry the same implication—that the direction of a city’s energy-system effect is set by whether the supply-side transition runs ahead of or behind the change in output composition, not by its level of economic development.

FIGURE 4

Such evident divergence in energy system transition is well supported by existing studies. The differentiated low carbon progress of power sectors in Hong Kong and Macao, together with the growing share of clean power in Guangdong Province (Zhang P. F. et al., 2022), is highly consistent with the huge gap between Macao’s CSI (−21.38%) and Shenzhen’s CSI (+4.57%) observed in this research. In addition, rational total carbon emission control can guide structural adjustment of energy-intensive sectors and accelerate the low-carbon upgrading of economic and industrial systems (Ren et al., 2022). From the perspective of technological diffusion, clean energy technology transfer exerts a significant inhibitory effect on regional carbon emissions within the Greater Bay Area, especially for local and cross-city technological cooperation (Zhou et al., 2025).

3.4.3 Tapio decoupling analysis and regional collaborative emission reduction potential

To place the growth–emission relationship on a formally recognised footing, the Tapio (2005) decoupling elasticity was computed for all eleven cities over 2016–2023 (Table 7).

Tapio decoupling elasticity and status of the eleven GBA cities, 2016–2023.

t = (%ΔCO2)/(%ΔGRP), following Tapio (2005). ΔGRP, is measured at current prices.

Three cities—Foshan, Zhongshan and Hong Kong—achieve strong decoupling, their CO2 emissions declining in absolute terms (ΔCO2 = −9.68%, −8.45% and −17.22%) while their economies expanded (ΔGRP = +63.74%, +42.05% and +39.39%), giving negative elasticities (t = −0.152, −0.201 and −0.437). Six cities—Guangzhou, Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Dongguan, Jiangmen and Zhaoqing—are weakly decoupled, with emissions growing more slowly than output (0.133 ≤ t ≤ 0.462). Only Huizhou (t = 0.863) and Macao (t = 1.000) fall into expansive coupling. No city shows strong negative decoupling, and in no city did emissions rise while output fell.

Foshan is the most striking case: its output carbon-intensity effect is simultaneously the largest negative contributor in the region (|CI| = 18.05%, against a growth effect of G = 15.99%), so the mitigation effect of falling carbon intensity has more than offset the upward pressure of economic expansion. This is the empirical basis for treating the manufacturing-transformation path as one that has already delivered decoupling.

The weakly decoupled group is internally heterogeneous. Guangzhou (t = 0.133), Dongguan (t = 0.136) and Jiangmen (t = 0.262) already show elasticities close to the strong-decoupling threshold, whereas Shenzhen (t = 0.462), Zhuhai (t = 0.404) and Zhaoqing (t = 0.282) continue to add emissions at a moderate rate. Because the region spans everything from strong decoupling to expansive coupling, it does not decouple uniformly; the resulting gradient is nevertheless ordered and interpretable, and it is this ordered heterogeneity that provides the basis for regional collaborative emission reduction.

This ordering is consistent with the international literature. Comparative evidence for the EU and the BRICS shows that the EU is dominated by strong decoupling while the BRICS are dominated by weak decoupling (Xie et al., 2025), which parallels the coexistence of strong and weak decoupling observed across the Greater Bay Area. Studies applying the same Tapio framework to China’s four provincial-level municipalities likewise report pronounced inter-city heterogeneity (Qiao and Wu, 2025).

Two caveats should be stated. First, because the pandemic falls inside the window and because Hong Kong and Macao were hit hardest, the decoupling status of the two Special Administrative Regions is sensitive to the period; the sub-period results are reported in Section 3.5.2. Second, GRP is measured at current prices (Section 2.4.3); since Tapio (2005) conventionally employs real growth, the elasticities reported here are lower bounds, and a real-price calculation would raise them and soften—though not reverse—the decoupling conclusions for the weakly decoupled cities. This is revisited as a limitation in Section 5.3.

3.5 Robustness checks

This section reports a set of robustness checks on the decomposition results: sensitivity to the decomposition method (Section 3.5.1), to the choice of sub-period (Section 3.5.2), to the exclusion of the three cities whose energy accounts follow a narrower boundary (Section 3.5.3), and to the emission-factor assumptions (Section 3.5.4), together with a cross-validation of the self-accounted emissions against the official inventory of Hong Kong (Section 3.5.5).

3.5.1 Robustness to the decomposition method

To ensure that our findings are not an artefact of the GDIM specification, we re-decomposed the identical emission series with the standard additive LMDI-I method under the Kaya identity C = P · PG · EI · CSI (Table 8). LMDI is used here not as an alternative to GDIM but as an independent benchmark: it rests on different structural assumptions, so agreement in the direction of each driver would show that this direction does not depend on the GDIM constraint structure.

The LMDI, decomposition is exact and its total coincides with that of the GDIM, decomposition; only the allocation among factors differs.

The LMDI decomposition is exact—the largest annual residual is about of CO2, numerically zero at the precision of the reported values—and its total coincides with that of the GDIM decomposition, whose own closure residual is reported in Supplementary Appendix D. For every factor common to the two methods, the sign of the contribution is identical across all eleven cities (11/11). The two frameworks allocate the same total change across different numbers of terms, so the magnitude of an individual contribution is not directly comparable between them, and the comparison is therefore used as a check on sign and direction rather than on magnitude. The qualitative conclusions—economic scale as the dominant driver, carbon and energy intensity as the principal mitigating effects, and Macao as the only city with a positive output carbon-intensity effect—are therefore reproduced by a method that shares none of the GDIM constraint structure, which is the purpose of the check. The eight-factor system is retained because the typology of Section 3.3 requires the absolute quantities and the composite ratios to be separated as distinct contributors, which the four-term Kaya chain cannot provide.

3.5.2 Temporal robustness

Within both sub-periods the economic-scale effect remains positive in every city and the output carbon-intensity effect remains negative in almost all of them—the exceptions being Huizhou in 2016–2019 (CI = +3.47%) and Dongguan in 2020–2023 (CI = +0.85%), as well as Macao in both sub-periods—so the dominant structure is preserved. Hong Kong shows the sharpest pandemic effect (economic-scale contribution of only 1.78% and a negative energy-scale contribution of −4.62% in 2020–2023). The full-period conclusions are therefore not driven by any single sub-period.

3.5.4 Robustness to emission-factor assumptions

The decomposition depends on the emission coefficients assigned to the principal energy carriers—coal (2.62), oil (2.25) and natural gas (2.10 tCO2/tce) — and on the electricity factor. To test whether the reported results are sensitive to these assumptions, we re-estimated the complete GDIM decomposition under eight scenarios, perturbing one coefficient at a time by ±10% (the electricity factor being perturbed around its annual values used in Section 2.4). Not a single sign changed: the economic-scale effect remains positive and both the output carbon-intensity and the energy carbon-intensity effects remain negative for every city, with Macao the only exception, so the qualitative pattern is unaffected. The largest change in any cumulative contribution rate is 2.9 percentage points (the energy-scale effect of Macao under the ±10% oil scenarios); for the other ten cities no factor moves by more than 2.3 percentage points. The descriptive statistics of Table 4 move by at most 1.08 percentage points and keep their extreme cities. Finally, the Ward. D2 clustering returns an identical partition in all eight scenarios (adjusted Rand index = 1.00), so the four-city typology is not an artefact of the assumed coefficients. Only the relative ordering of cities whose contribution rates are nearly tied shifts marginally; our interpretation is therefore framed in terms of the extremes and the typology rather than of small ordinal differences between individual cities.

Over 2015–2023 the two series move almost in parallel: the correlation coefficient reaches r = 0.98, and their peak year is identical (2016). The self-accounted values exceed the official figures by a stable margin of about 12%, with the ratio confined to a narrow band of 1.07–1.15 (mean 1.12, standard deviation 0.02). An offset that is stable in both sign and size across the whole period points to a difference in accounting boundary rather than to year-to-year estimation error; and because the decomposition operates on annual changes rather than on levels, an offset of this kind cancels out and does not affect the results. These cross-checks indicate that the self-accounted series reproduce both the trend and the magnitude of the official emissions of Hong Kong. No comparable official city-level CO2 inventory is publicly available for the nine mainland cities, so the self-accounted series is adopted to ensure internal consistency.

4 Discussion

4.1 Interpretation of heterogeneous driving-factor mechanisms across cities

A mechanism-level reading of the Shenzhen case illustrates how the composition of output conditions the direction of the energy-system effect. Where a city’s industrial base is organised around electricity-intensive, high-value-added manufacturing, output growth tends to raise the demand for power faster than the supply side can be decarbonised, so the energy-supply margin tends to become the binding constraint. Mitigation in such cities may therefore depend less on local fuel switching than on the cleanliness and stability of imported electricity, which makes regional power-grid coordination an important enabling condition for their own decarbonisation.

Cross-city disparities in per capita carbon emissions track differences in economic structure and industrial composition (Figure 5). Because the per capita indicator is an aggregate ratio, household-level behaviour cannot be separated from it (Section 5.3); public engagement and the development of low-carbon lifestyles remain relevant prerequisites for a society-wide low-carbon transition (Zuo, 2023; Xia and Huang, 2023), and the growing share of small households (one- and two-person families) has been identified in the literature as a micro driver of residential energy consumption (Fu et al., 2021). These factors remain an open question for micro-level research.

FIGURE 5

Inter-city heterogeneity can be further explained by divergent institutional and historical development trajectories. The nine mainland cities and the two SARs have experienced distinct industrialisation and energy-system evolution over recent decades. Hong Kong and Macao completed industrial restructuring earlier, with manufacturing largely relocated to the mainland Pearl River Delta; their current energy demand is dominated by commercial, transport and service sectors, which differs greatly from manufacturing-intensive cities such as Foshan and Dongguan. For the mainland cities, differences in the timing of reform and economic opening, in the timing of industrial transfer and in policy support have shaped uneven economic scales, energy endowments and structural and efficiency-related capabilities. Such historical and institutional differences complement the GDIM decomposition results and help explain why a single uniform emission-reduction policy is unlikely to be equally effective across the GBA urban agglomeration.

4.2 Comparative analysis with previous research findings

The four-category urban classification in this study complements existing urban typology research. International studies typically classify Chinese cities into industrial, commercial and mixed types based on economic attributes (Ramaswami et al., 2018), which resonates with the economic-scale driven and carbon-intensity suppression types identified here. Traffic-based urban classification applied in the San Francisco Bay Area also illustrates the feasibility of multi-dimensional urban grouping (Kuncheria et al., 2025). Studies of China have adopted K-means clustering to divide Guangdong’s prefecture-level cities into four low-carbon types (Zhong et al., 2021), and structural heterogeneity across cities has been widely documented in urban agglomeration research (Li M. et al., 2024).

Different from previous classifications relying on total carbon emission levels, this study classifies cities based on factor contribution structures, focusing on how emission changes are composed within cities. Traditional classifications reflect external disparities in urban development stages, whereas this study highlights differences in emission driving mechanisms. Compared with trade-based production–consumption city typologies (Mi et al., 2016), the proposed framework describes urban heterogeneity in terms of structural composition and temporal evolution, offering an empirical basis for differentiated carbon mitigation policy formulation.

This study’s findings show both consistency and divergence with existing Greater Bay Area-related decomposition research. The corroborating evidence is reported in Section 3.1; the divergences arise mainly from differences in city coverage, observation window and decomposition method.

First, most previous studies covered only the nine mainland GBA cities and excluded Hong Kong and Macao (Ming et al., 2024), whereas this study incorporates the complete “9 + 2” city cluster; including these service-oriented special administrative regions, with their distinctive energy systems, enriches the heterogeneity analysis. Second, this study extends the research period to 2023, covering the post-pandemic recovery and the early dual-carbon implementation stage, whereas most earlier studies terminated their observation before 2021 (Wang et al., 2026), which generates discrepancies in the estimated contribution characteristics. Third, this study employs the GDIM model, which accounts for the inherent correlations among variables, whereas the conventional approach is LMDI; such methodological differences redistribute factor contributions and partly explain the divergences observed.

4.3 Theoretical basis for regional collaborative emission-reduction

Heterogeneous decoupling statuses reflect urban complementary advantages and provide a basis for regional collaborative emission reduction. In principle, complementary resource endowments and functional positioning can lower the cost of regional decarbonisation and help balance equity and efficiency. Industrial restructuring and efficiency improvement are identified in the literature as core drivers of strong decoupling (Li and Xiao, 2026), which aligns with the transition path of cities such as Foshan and Zhongshan, whose decoupling elasticities are −0.152 and −0.201.

Notably, theoretical complementary advantages cannot be directly transformed into effective regional collaboration. The GBA involves three customs territories, two legal systems and multi-level administrative governance, creating institutional barriers to cross-regional policy coordination. Differences in fiscal capacity, environmental regulation intensity and industrial policy orientation further hinder a unified cost–benefit allocation for collaborative emission reduction. For example, developing peripheral cities may regard strict carbon constraints as barriers to economic growth, while the region’s leading cities may lack incentives for low-carbon technology transfer without reasonable benefit compensation. Effective regional collaboration therefore requires systematic institutional design, benefit-sharing mechanisms and a clear division of responsibilities. Accordingly, this study offers a three-tier policy discussion that could help match differentiated urban transition demands and address cross-regional coordination dilemmas.

5 Conclusions and policy implications

5.1 Main research conclusions

Based on empirical decomposition and mechanism analysis, this study adopts the GDIM to investigate carbon emission driving mechanisms across 11 cities in the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA) during 2016–2023, yielding four main conclusions.

First, economic growth and carbon-intensity reduction constitute the two dominant components of the region’s emission change. These contributions are associational decompositions of accounting identities and do not imply causality. Economic scale (G) is positively associated with carbon emissions, while output carbon intensity (CI) serves as the primary mitigating factor, forming a gradient across the region’s cities. Foshan and Zhongshan record strong decoupling, their growth and intensity effects nearly offsetting (t = −0.152 and −0.201), and Hong Kong records the largest negative elasticity in the region (t = −0.437); Shenzhen and Guangzhou display a high-growth, high-mitigation pattern; Huizhou is dominated by economic expansion with insufficient carbon constraints; and Macao, with a positive CI value, exhibits a distinctive decline in carbon productivity alongside economic growth.

Second, the driving-structure classification distinguishes four types in the GBA. Carbon-intensity suppression cities (Guangzhou, Foshan, Zhongshan and Hong Kong) combine the strongest intensity effect in the sample (CI = −15.90% on average) with negative per capita carbon effects. Economic-scale driven cities (Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Dongguan, Jiangmen and Zhaoqing) pair the highest economic-scale effect among the multi-city groups (G = 21.39%) with a weaker intensity response, and they span the full range of the innovation index reported in Section 3.3.5. Huizhou constitutes an energy-scale expansion type (E = 26.15%, PC = 19.95%, CI = −3.25%), and Macao a specialized service-structure type whose combination of energy expansion, rising carbon intensity and strongly negative per capita output and energy-intensity effects has no analogue among the manufacturing-oriented cities.

Third, per capita carbon emissions (PC) and the energy-system indicators account for much of the variation in reduction effects across cities. PC is an aggregate ratio and is therefore read alongside each city’s industrial and energy structure (Section 5.3); it is markedly uneven, dominating the positive side in Huizhou (PC = 19.95%) and remaining positive in Macao and in most of the economic-scale driven cities, while curbing per capita carbon pressure in Foshan, Zhongshan and Hong Kong (PC between −6.6% and −6.8%). The contrast in energy-structure carbon intensity (CSI) between Shenzhen (+4.57%, the only positive value in the region) and Macao (−21.38%) points to different stages of the energy transition and to conditions on which a regional collaborative framework could build.

Fourth, the analytical sequence adopted here—decomposition of the driving structure, classification of cities by that structure, and identification of the factors that matter most—may also be applicable to other urban agglomerations, although its transferability is not tested here. The study illustrates the applicability of GDIM to multi-factor, strongly correlated and structurally heterogeneous carbon-emission systems, and shows how quantitative decomposition results can be linked to policy discussion.

5.2 Policy implications

The following measures are indicative directions derived from the decomposition results. Their feasibility depends on local institutional, fiscal and data conditions, and would require further ex-ante assessment before implementation. They illustrate how the empirical findings can inform policy design.

5.2.1 Tier 1: differentiated regulation

Carbon-intensity suppression cities (Guangzhou, Foshan, Zhongshan and Hong Kong) could consolidate the intensity margin that defines them, maintaining dual constraints on carbon emission quantity and intensity and reinforcing the mitigation that has already delivered the region’s strongest decoupling. Led by provincial authorities, a manufacturing green transformation alliance could be established to replicate Foshan’s experience, with fiscal and tax incentives for industrial parks and enterprises that achieve effective carbon offsetting through intensity reduction. Hong Kong, whose driving structure places it with these cities rather than with Macao, seems better matched by intensity-oriented instruments; its energy-scale effect is already negative (E = −4.07%), so volume-based instruments are no longer the binding lever.

Economic-scale driven cities (Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Dongguan, Jiangmen and Zhaoqing) could align the pace of expansion with the intensity response. Shenzhen, whose energy-structure carbon intensity is the only positive value in the region, faces its binding constraint on the energy-supply margin: green power procurement ratios and the share of external clean energy supply could be incorporated into its assessment systems to ease this structural carbon pressure.

Huizhou, the energy-scale expansion type, would be better served by mechanisms that keep new growth on a low-carbon path and avoid high-carbon lock-in. Strict carbon evaluation for new projects and industrial planning would be required, matched with distributed new energy deployment. Green urbanisation policies could curb the growth of per capita carbon emissions, which are the highest in the region (PC = 19.95%).

Macao, the specialized service-structure type, would need instruments matched to its exceptional profile (E = 42.06%, CI = +16.93%, CSI = −21.38%): explicit energy-consumption ceilings and refined energy management, shifting from extensive energy consumption towards refined low-carbon governance.

5.2.2 Tier 2: collaborative governance

The GBA could consider building a unified regional green technology transfer and certification platform. Standardized green technology catalogues and certification criteria would facilitate the transfer of mature low-carbon technologies from cities that have already decoupled to those whose carbon pressure is still rising.

A regional green power trading mechanism could be piloted. Green power packages drawing on Yunnan–Guizhou hydropower and Guangdong offshore wind could be supplied to cities facing a rising energy-structure carbon intensity, such as Shenzhen.

A special GBA carbon neutrality development fund could be considered. Jointly funded by the region’s core cities and provincial finance, the fund could support low-carbon infrastructure in peripheral cities and subsidise cross-city green cooperation projects.

5.2.3 Tier 3: data support

Unified regional carbon accounting standards could be developed. Guangdong’s statistical departments, together with the Hong Kong and Macao authorities, could formulate common GBA urban greenhouse-gas accounting guidelines, adopting consistent emission factors for fossil fuels and region-specific electricity coefficients to address inconsistencies in statistical scope and definitions.

A long-term monitoring and evaluation system for carbon driving factors could be developed based on the GDIM framework. Regular updates of factor contribution rates and of the urban typology would support periodic tracking of regional carbon structural change, improving the relevance and adaptability of low-carbon policy formulation.

Taken together, these three tiers illustrate how the empirical findings of this study could inform policy design across the GBA’s low-carbon transition.

5.3 Limitations and future prospects

This study has several limitations that indicate directions for further research. First, data limitations exist. Restricted by public statistical data, partial energy consumption statistics of several cities only cover industrial sectors, which may affect the accurate identification of overall carbon driving structures. Future research can supplement multi-sector energy and enterprise micro-data to optimize the accounting system.

Second, the GDIM method adopted in this study provides static retrospective decomposition of historical emission changes, lacking dynamic scenario simulation. Subsequent studies can combine system dynamics or CGE models to predict carbon emission evolution trends under diverse collaborative emission reduction scenarios.

Third, this study focuses on territorial direct and electricity-related indirect emissions, ignoring embodied carbon emissions in cross-regional supply chains. Future research can adopt multi-regional input-output models to re-evaluate GBA carbon footprints from a consumption-based perspective.

Fourth, two measurement caveats should be noted. Electricity emission factors are applied in the model on a standard-coal-equivalent basis, as are the other energy types, and their year-to-year variation follows the officially published annual grid emission factors; were electricity-related emissions instead computed on a terminal-electricity (kWh) basis, the absolute magnitude of the electricity component would be adjusted accordingly, although this does not materially alter the relative contributions that are the focus of the decomposition. In addition, the per capita indicator used here is an aggregate ratio based on territorial emissions and cannot isolate residential consumption; household-level analysis would require survey or micro-data that are beyond the scope of this study.

Fifth, the decoupling elasticities reported in Section 3.4.3 are computed from GRP at current prices, whereas Tapio (2005) conventionally uses real growth. The elasticities are therefore lower bounds: a real-price calculation would raise them and would soften, though not reverse, the decoupling conclusions for the weakly decoupled cities.
